cards.grammarNote:
Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article agrees:
**el** (masc.) · **la** (fem.) → **el pan** (bread), **la leche** (milk). Most **-o** words are masculine, most **-a** feminine — but learn each noun with its article.
cards.englishPhrase: The bread is here, the milk is there.
cards.phrase: El pan está aquí, la leche está allí.

table.title: Definite articles agree with gender & number
table.note: Most -o words are masculine, most -a feminine — learn each noun with its article.

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish usually **drops the subject pronoun** — the verb ending already shows who the subject is.
**Soy estudiante** = **Yo soy estudiante**. Add **yo/tú/él** only for emphasis or contrast.

table.title: ser — the subject pronoun is optional
table.note: The ending already shows who — add yo/tú/él only for emphasis.

cards.grammarNote:
Adjectives agree in gender and number with who they describe:
**él está nervioso** / **ella está nerviosa** / **ellos están nerviosos**. Change the ending **-o** (masc.) ↔ **-a** (fem.), add **-s** for plural.

produce.concept: Adjectives match the noun they modify
produce.task: he is nervous, she is nervous
produce.answer: él está nervioso, ella está nerviosa

cards.english: I am a doctor. (no article before jobs)
cards.grammarNote:
State a profession with **ser** and **no article**:
**soy médico** (I'm a doctor), **es profesora** (she's a teacher). Add an article only with a description: **es un buen médico** (he's a good doctor).

cards.english: The bank is nearby. (estar for location)
cards.grammarNote:
Location always uses **estar**, even for permanent buildings:
**el banco está cerca** (the bank is nearby), **¿dónde está el baño?** (where's the bathroom?). Never **es** for location.

cloze.prompt: the bank is nearby (location → estar)

cards.english: The food is delicious. (estar for taste)
cards.grammarNote:
Use **estar** (not **ser**) for how food tastes right now — a temporary state:
**la comida está deliciosa** (the food is delicious), **el café está frío** (the coffee is cold). **ser** would sound like a permanent trait.

b.gloss: a good soup in general → ser

a.gloss: I feel happy right now — a mood (estar)

b.gloss: I'm a happy person — a trait (ser)

cards.grammarNote:
Feelings and moods use **estar** — they're temporary states:
**estoy feliz** (I'm happy), **estoy triste** (I'm sad). **ser feliz** exists too, but describes being a happy person in general.

cards.english: There's a bank / The bank is here (hay vs estar)
cards.word: hay un banco / el banco está aquí
cards.grammarNote:
**hay** introduces something that exists (indefinite): **hay un banco cerca**. **estar** locates something already known (definite): **el banco está en la esquina**.
Rule of thumb: **hay** + un/una/números; **estar** + el/la/mi/este.
cards.englishPhrase: There's a pharmacy nearby, and the pharmacy is on the corner.
cards.phrase: Hay una farmacia cerca, y la farmacia está en la esquina.

a.gloss: a bank exists / introduces it → hay

b.gloss: the known bank is located here → estar

cards.grammarNote:
**hay** = there is / there are — one word for both singular and plural:
**hay pan** (there's bread), **hay dos manzanas** (there are two apples). It never changes form.

table.title: hay — there is / there are (invariable)
table.note: One form for all — hay never changes.

cards.english: you (formal — to a stranger or elder)
cards.grammarNote:
Two words for 'you': **tú** (informal — friends, kids) · **usted** (formal — strangers, elders, bosses).
**usted** takes the **él/ella** verb form: **usted tiene**, not *usted tienes*.

Spanish **has** a feeling where English **is** one — use **tener**, not ser/estar:
**tengo hambre** (hungry) · **tengo sed** (thirsty) · **tengo frío/calor** (cold/hot) · **tengo miedo** (afraid) · **tengo 20 años** (I'm 20).

table.title: Physical states use tener (‘to have’)
table.note: Spanish ‘has’ the state where English ‘is’ it — not ser/estar.

cards.grammarNote:
Some feelings use **tener** (to have), not **estar**:
**tengo miedo** (I'm afraid), **tengo celos** (I'm jealous), **tengo sueño** (I'm sleepy). Literally 'I have fear/jealousy/sleepiness'.

table.title: More tener idioms (not estar)
table.note: Literally ‘I have fear / sleep / hurry…’.

cards.english: I have cold hands. (tener + article + agreement)
cards.grammarNote:
Describe your body with **tener** + article + adjective (which agrees):
**tengo las manos frías** (my hands are cold, lit. 'I have the hands cold'), **tiene los ojos azules** (she has blue eyes).

cloze.prompt: my hands are cold (las manos = fem. pl.)

cards.english: I like coffee. (gustar works in reverse)
cards.grammarNote:
**gustar** literally means 'to please' — the thing liked is the subject:
**me gusta el café** = 'coffee pleases me'. Use **gusta** for one thing, **gustan** for plural: **me gustan las manzanas**.
cards.phrase: Me gusta el té, ¿y a ti?

table.title: gustar — ‘to please’ (works backwards)
table.note: One thing → gusta; plural things → gustan (me gustan las uvas).

cards.grammarNote:
To say you like doing something, use **me gusta** + the infinitive:
**me gusta leer** (I like reading), **me gusta correr** (I like running). Stays singular **gusta** before a verb.

cloze.prompt: I like reading (a verb → stays singular)

cards.english: My head hurts. (me duele — like gustar)
cards.grammarNote:
**doler** (to hurt) works like **gustar** — the body part is the subject:
**me duele la cabeza** (my head hurts), **me duelen los pies** (my feet hurt — plural **duelen**). Uses the article, not 'my'.

table.title: doler — works like gustar
table.note: Body part is the subject → duele / duelen; use the article, not ‘my’.

cards.english: What's your name? (lit. how do you call yourself)
cards.grammarNote:
Names use the reflexive verb **llamarse** ('to call oneself'):
**me llamo** (I call myself) · **te llamas** (you call yourself) · **se llama** (he/she calls him/herself).
cards.englishPhrase: What's your name? — My name is Ana.

table.title: llamarse — ‘to call oneself’ (names)
table.note: ¿Cómo te llamas? = What's your name?

cards.grammarNote:
With body parts, Spanish uses the **definite article** (el/la/los/las), not a possessive — the reflexive pronoun already shows whose:
**me lavo las manos** (I wash my hands), **le duele la cabeza** (his head hurts). Not *mis manos*.

contrast.prompt: ‘I wash my hands’ — las or mis?

a.gloss: ✓ reflexive already shows it's yours → article

cards.grammarNote:
**sentirse** (to feel) is reflexive — the pronoun matches the subject:
**me siento** (I feel), **te sientes** (you feel), **se siente** (he/she feels). In **me siento cansado/cansada** the adjective still agrees.
cards.englishPhrase: How do you feel? — I feel great.

table.title: sentirse — ‘to feel’ (reflexive, e→ie)
table.note: Adjective still agrees: me siento cansado / cansada.

cards.grammarNote:
Two mandatory contractions before masculine **el**:
**a + el → al** (Voy **al** parque), **de + el → del** (la puerta **del** hotel). They don't contract with **la/los/las**.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to the market from the office.
cards.phrase: Voy al mercado desde la oficina.

produce.concept: el contracts: a + el → al, de + el → del
produce.task: I'm going to the park; the hotel door
produce.answer: voy al parque; la puerta del hotel
produce.gloss: Only masculine singular el contracts — never la/los/las.

cards.english: I'm going to the park. (ir a + place)
cards.grammarNote:
**ir a** + place = to go to a place; remember **a + el → al**:
**voy al parque** (I go to the park), **vamos a la playa** (we go to the beach). Also **ir a** + infinitive = near future: **voy a comer**.
cards.englishPhrase: We're going to the beach today.

cards.grammarNote:
The present progressive = **estar** + gerund (**-ando** / **-iendo**):
**estoy nadando** (I'm swimming), **estoy comiendo** (I'm eating). Only for actions happening right now.

table.title: Present progressive: estar + gerund
table.note: estoy nadando = I'm swimming (right now).

table.title: querer — to want (e→ie)
table.note: Stem e→ie in the stressed forms; nosotros keeps the e.

cards.grammarNote:
**querer** is a stem-changing verb: e→ie in the stressed forms.
**quiero · quieres · quiere · queremos · quieren** — note **nosotros queremos** keeps the **e** (unstressed).

**la mano** is feminine even though it ends in **-o** — a classic exception:
**la mano derecha** (the right hand). Other tricky ones: **el día** (masc., ends -a), **el problema** (masc.).

table.title: Gender exceptions
table.note: These break the -o/-a rule; memorize them.

cards.english: I work as a nurse. (trabajar de/como)
cards.grammarNote:
**trabajar de** or **trabajar como** = to work as (a job):
**trabajo de enfermero** (I work as a nurse), **trabajo en un hospital** (I work in a hospital — **en** for the place).
cards.englishPhrase: I work as a cook in a restaurant.
cards.phrase: Trabajo de cocinero en un restaurante.

table.title: Talking about your job
table.note: de / como = work AS; en = work IN / at a place.

cards.grammarNote:
To conjugate a regular **-AR** verb in the present tense, drop the **-ar** ending and add the personal ending.

**hablar → habl-** + ending:

**-o** (yo), **-as** (tú), **-a** (él/ella), **-amos** (nosotros), **-an** (ellos/ellas)

table.title: hablar (to speak) — present tense
table.note: The endings -o / -as / -a / -amos / -an apply to ALL regular -AR verbs: trabajar, comprar, caminar, cocinar, nadar, viajar, ayudar, enseñar, practicar.

cards.grammarNote:
To conjugate a regular **-ER** verb in the present tense, drop the **-er** ending and add the personal ending.

**comer → com-** + ending:

**-o** (yo), **-es** (tú), **-e** (él/ella), **-emos** (nosotros), **-en** (ellos/ellas)

Notice: the yo ending **-o** is the same as -AR, but tú/él/nosotros use **-e-** instead of **-a-**.

table.title: comer (to eat) — present tense
table.note: The same endings apply to all regular -ER verbs: aprender, vender.

cards.grammarNote:
To conjugate a regular **-IR** verb in the present tense, drop the **-ir** ending and add the personal ending.

**vivir → viv-** + ending:

**-o** (yo), **-es** (tú), **-e** (él/ella), **-imos** (nosotros), **-en** (ellos/ellas)

-IR verbs share four endings with -ER verbs. The **only** difference is nosotros: **-imos** (not -emos).
cards.phrase: Ellos viven cerca de la escuela.

table.title: vivir (to live) — present tense
table.note: The same endings apply to all regular -IR verbs: escribir.

cards.english: -AR present tense: yo form of trabajar
cards.grammarNote:
For regular **-AR** verbs, the **yo** (I) form always ends in **-o**.

**trabajar → trabaj-** + **o** = **trabajo**

This pattern is the same for all regular -AR verbs: yo hablo, yo compro, yo camino, yo cocino...

cloze.prompt: Fill in the correct present-tense form of trabajar (yo).

cards.english: -AR present tense: full conjugation of estudiar
cards.grammarNote:
Regular **-AR** verb pattern applied to **estudiar**:

**estudiar → estudi-** + personal ending

**yo** estudio · **tú** estudias · **él/ella** estudia · **nosotros** estudiamos · **ellos/ellas** estudian
cards.phrase: Nosotros estudiamos español en la escuela.

produce.task: Give the present-tense form of estudiar for each person: yo / tú / él-ella / nosotros / ellos-ellas.

cards.english: -ER vs -IR endings: identical except nosotros (-emos vs -imos)
cards.grammarNote:
-ER and -IR verbs share **four** of their five present-tense endings.

The **only** difference is the nosotros form: **-emos** for -ER verbs (comemos), **-imos** for -IR verbs (vivimos).

Every other ending — -o, -es, -e, -en — is identical.
cards.englishPhrase: We eat at home. / We live at home.
cards.phrase: Nosotros comemos en casa. / Nosotros vivimos en casa.

contrast.prompt: -ER vs -IR in the nosotros form — which ending is correct?

cards.english: Irregular yo forms — regular everywhere except yo
cards.word: tengo, hago, salgo, veo, doy, sé
cards.grammarNote:
Some verbs are **regular in every person except yo**. The yo form is irregular; all other forms follow normal -ar/-er/-ir endings.

**tengo** (tener), **hago** (hacer), **salgo** (salir), **veo** (ver), **doy** (dar), **sé** (saber)

table.title: Irregular yo forms (regular everywhere else)
table.note: All other persons (tú, él, nosotros…) are regular for these verbs.

cards.grammarNote:
**hacer** (to do/make) is regular for tú, él, nosotros, ellos — but the **yo form is hago**, not *haco*.

Many verbs share this **-go** yo shape (tengo, salgo…).

cloze.prompt: What is the yo form of hacer? (I make the food.)

cards.english: SER vs ESTAR — present tense side by side
cards.grammarNote:
Both **ser** and **estar** mean *to be* but are not interchangeable.

**ser** → identity, permanent traits (who/what something fundamentally is).
**estar** → states, locations, conditions (how something is right now).

*Él es español* (identity) vs *Él está en la oficina* (location).
cards.englishPhrase: She is a student; she is at school.
cards.phrase: Ella es estudiante; ella está en la escuela.

table.title: SER · ESTAR — present (identity vs state)
table.note: Left column = ser (identity/permanent). Right column = estar (state/location).

cards.english: IR, TENER, VENIR — three high-frequency irregulars
cards.grammarNote:
These three verbs are extremely common and irregular in the present.

**ir** (to go): voy, vas, va, vamos, van
**tener** (to have): tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen
**venir** (to come): vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, vienen

**tener** and **venir** share the **-go** yo form; **ir** uses a completely different stem (*v-*).
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the restaurant; I have a coffee.
cards.phrase: Voy al restaurante; tengo un café.

table.title: IR · TENER · VENIR — present
table.note: Columns in order: ir · tener · venir.

cards.english: Produce irregular yo forms — tener, hacer, salir, ver, dar
cards.grammarNote:
Give the **yo form** for each verb. All other persons are regular — only yo is irregular.

**tener→tengo**, **hacer→hago**, **salir→salgo**, **ver→veo**, **dar→doy**
cards.englishPhrase: I have, I do, I leave, I see, I give.

produce.concept: Irregular yo forms in the present tense
produce.task: Give the yo (I) form of each verb: tener, hacer, salir, ver, dar
produce.gloss: only the yo form is irregular — all other persons follow regular endings

cards.grammarNote:
**querer** (to want) is an e→ie stem-changer.

The stem vowel **e** becomes **ie** in all forms **except nosotros**, which keeps the original stem.

Same pattern: **pensar** (pienso), **empezar** (empiezo), **entender** (entiendo).

table.title: querer (e→ie)
table.note: nosotros keeps the original stem — no change. pensar → pienso, empezar → empiezo follow the same boot pattern.

cards.grammarNote:
**poder** (to be able to / can) is an o→ue stem-changer.

The stem vowel **o** becomes **ue** in all forms **except nosotros**.

Same pattern: **encontrar** (encuentro). Special case: **jugar** changes **u→ue** (juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, juegan).

table.title: poder (o→ue)
table.note: nosotros keeps the original stem. encontrar → encuentro follows the same pattern. jugar is special: u→ue (juego).

cards.grammarNote:
**pensar** (to think) follows the e→ie pattern.

In the **yo** form the stem vowel **e** shifts to **ie**: **pienso**.

*penso* is not a Spanish word — the stem must change.

cloze.prompt: I think (e→ie) — the yo form of pensar

cards.grammarNote:
**encontrar** (to find) follows the o→ue pattern.

In the **yo** form the stem vowel **o** shifts to **ue**: **encuentro**.

*encontro* is not a Spanish word — the stem must change.

cloze.prompt: I find (o→ue) — the yo form of encontrar

cards.english: The boot pattern: stem changes vs. nosotros
cards.grammarNote:
Stem-changing verbs form a **"boot" (or "shoe") shape** on the conjugation chart.

The stem changes in **yo, tú, él/ella, ellos** — the four forms that make the outline of a boot.

**nosotros** sits outside the boot and **always keeps the original stem** — no change.

contrast.prompt: Which form keeps the original stem?

b.gloss: stem stays as e — nosotros is always outside the boot

cards.grammarNote: The **preterite** is the narrative past — a single, completed action seen as finished. Regular **-ar** verbs take the endings **-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron**. Only **yo** and **él/ella** carry a written accent.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I worked at the office.

table.title: Preterite: -ar verbs (trabajar)
table.note: Accents only on trabajé and trabajó.

cards.grammarNote: **-er** and **-ir** verbs share the *same* preterite endings: **-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron**. So comer and vivir conjugate identically.
cards.englishPhrase: Last night I ate at the restaurant.

table.title: Preterite: -er / -ir (comer, vivir)
table.note: -er and -ir are identical in the preterite.

cards.grammarNote: For a finished, one-time action use the preterite. The **él/ella** form of an -ar verb ends in **-ó** (cocinó), never the present **-a** (cocina).

cloze.prompt: she cooked dinner (finished action → preterite)

cards.english: I went to the park. (ir → fui)
cards.grammarNote: **ser** and **ir** have the *same* irregular preterite: **fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron** — context tells them apart. **Fui al parque** = I went; **fui médico** = I was a doctor.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I went to the park.

table.title: Preterite: ser AND ir (identical)
table.note: No accents. Context decides 'went' vs 'was'.

cards.english: I was at home last night. (estar → estuve)
cards.grammarNote: A group of irregulars takes a new stem + the endings **-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron** (no accents): **estar→estuv-, tener→tuv-, poder→pud-**. So: estuve, tuve, pude.
cards.englishPhrase: Last night I was at home.

table.title: Irregular preterite (new stem, -e/-o)
table.note: Endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron. No accent on yo/él.

cards.grammarNote: More irregular stems, same **-e/-o** endings: **hacer→hic-** (but **hizo** with z), **decir→dij-** (dijeron, no i), **venir→vin-**.

table.title: Irregular preterite (hacer, decir, venir)
table.note: hizo spelled with z; dijeron drops the i.

cards.english: Say the preterite 'yo' form. (I ate / drank / lived)
cards.grammarNote: The **yo** preterite of regular -er/-ir verbs ends in a stressed **-í**: comer→comí, beber→bebí, vivir→viví.
cards.englishPhrase: I ate, I drank, I lived.

produce.concept: Preterite = one finished action in the past
produce.task: I ate, I drank, I lived

cards.english: As a child I used to swim. (imperfect, -ar)
cards.grammarNote: The **imperfect** is the 'used to / was ‑ing' past — habits and background, no clear end. Regular **-ar** verbs take **-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban**.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I used to swim at the beach.
cards.phrase: De niño nadaba en la playa.

table.title: Imperfect: -ar verbs (nadar)
table.note: yo and él/ella are identical: nadaba.

cards.english: As a child I used to eat a lot of bread. (imperfect, -er/-ir)
cards.grammarNote: **-er** and **-ir** verbs share the imperfect endings **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían** — every form carries an accent on the **í**.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I used to eat a lot of bread.

table.title: Imperfect: -er / -ir (comer, vivir)
table.note: Accent on every í. -er and -ir identical.

cards.english: As a child I was happy. (ser → era)
cards.grammarNote: The imperfect has only **three** irregular verbs: **ser→era, ir→iba, ver→veía**. Learn these; everything else is regular.
cards.englishPhrase: As a child I was happy.

table.title: The 3 irregular imperfects
table.note: The ONLY irregular imperfect verbs.

cards.english: She always cooked at home. (habit → imperfect)
cards.grammarNote: Words like **siempre** (always) and **nunca** (never) signal a repeated habit → use the **imperfect** (cocinaba), not the preterite (cocinó).

cloze.prompt: she always cooked (repeated habit → imperfect)

cards.english: Say the imperfect. (I used to work / she used to study)
cards.grammarNote: Imperfect = 'used to' or 'would' (habitual). -ar yo/él ends in **-aba**: trabajaba, estudiaba.
cards.englishPhrase: I used to work, she used to study.

produce.concept: Imperfect = used to / would (a past habit)
produce.task: I used to work, she used to study

cards.english: I ate out — once vs. every day.
cards.grammarNote: Same verb, two pasts: **preterite** = one finished event; **imperfect** = a repeated habit or ongoing background. **Comí** (I ate, that once) vs **comía** (I used to eat).
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I ate out; as a child I ate at home.
cards.phrase: Ayer comí en el restaurante; de niño comía en casa.

cards.grammarNote: The time expression usually decides the tense. **ayer, anoche, la semana pasada** → a finished point → **preterite**. **siempre, de niño** → a habit → **imperfect**.
cards.englishPhrase: Yesterday I worked; as a child I worked here.

table.title: Which past does the time word want?
table.note: A fixed point → preterite; a habit → imperfect.

cards.english: I was cooking when she arrived. (background + event)
cards.grammarNote: For an interrupted scene, the ongoing background is **imperfect** (cocinaba) and the event that cuts in is **preterite** (llegó). English 'was ‑ing' → imperfect.
cards.englishPhrase: I was cooking when she arrived.

cloze.prompt: I was cooking (ongoing) when she arrived

cards.english: I arrived, cooked, and ate. (a chain of events)
cards.grammarNote: A sequence of completed actions, each moving the story forward, is all **preterite**: llegué, cociné, comí. (Note llegar → **llegué** keeps the hard g with -ué.)
cards.englishPhrase: I arrived, I cooked, and I ate.

produce.concept: A chain of finished actions → all preterite
produce.task: I arrived, I cooked, and I ate
produce.gloss: each completed step moves the story → preterite

cards.english: Tomorrow I'm going to study at home. (near/planned future: ir a + infinitive)
cards.word: mañana voy a estudiar en casa
cards.grammarNote: The **near future** is **ir a + infinitive**: conjugate *ir* (voy, vas, va, vamos, van) and add **a** plus an unchanged infinitive. It's the most common way to talk about plans in speech.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I'm going to study at home.
cards.phrase: Mañana voy a estudiar en casa.

table.title: ir a + infinitive (near future)
table.note: Only ir changes; the infinitive stays the same.

cards.english: Tomorrow I will speak with María. (simple future)
cards.grammarNote: The **simple future** adds one set of endings to the *whole infinitive* — same for -ar, -er, -ir: **-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án**. hablar → hablaré, comer → comeré, vivir → viviré.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will speak with María.

table.title: Simple future (endings on the infinitive)
table.note: Same endings for -ar/-er/-ir. Accent on every form except nosotros.

cards.english: Tomorrow I will eat at the restaurant. (future -er)
cards.grammarNote: Future endings attach to the **full infinitive**, so -er/-ir verbs work the same way: comer → **comeré**, vivir → **viviré**.
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will eat at the restaurant.

cloze.prompt: I will eat (future)

cards.english: Tomorrow I will have to work. (irregular future stems)
cards.grammarNote: Some verbs use an **irregular future stem** but take the **normal endings**: tener→**tendr-**, poder→**podr-**, salir→**saldr-**, hacer→**har-**, decir→**dir-**. So tener → tendré, tendrás, tendrá...
cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will have to work.

table.title: Irregular future stems (+ normal endings)
table.note: Stem changes, but the endings (-é, -ás, -á...) are the same.

cards.english: going to eat vs. will eat
cards.grammarNote: **ir a + infinitive** = a near, planned future (very common in speech). The **simple future** (-é) feels a bit more distant or formal. Both are correct.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to eat now; tomorrow I will eat at home.
cards.phrase: Voy a comer ahora; mañana comeré en casa.

cards.english: Say the future 'yo' form. (I will eat / drink / live)
cards.grammarNote: The **yo** future ends in a stressed **-é** on the full infinitive: comer→comeré, beber→beberé, vivir→viviré.
cards.englishPhrase: I will eat, I will drink, I will live.

produce.task: I will eat, I will drink, I will live

cards.english: He's probably at home. (future of probability / a guess about the present)
cards.grammarNote: The **future** can express **probability about the present** — a guess, not a plan. *Está en casa* = I know he's home; *estará en casa* = he's **probably** home. Often answers ¿Dónde estará? (Where can he be?).
cards.englishPhrase: He is at home (I know); he's probably at home (a guess).

cards.englishPhrase: Tomorrow I will go to the park.

cloze.prompt: I will go (future)

cards.grammarNote: The **conditional** ('would') adds one set of endings to the *whole infinitive* — same for -ar/-er/-ir: **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían**. hablar → hablaría.

table.title: Conditional (endings on the infinitive)
table.note: Accent on every í. yo and él/ella match.

cards.english: I would eat at the restaurant. (conditional -er)
cards.grammarNote: Conditional endings attach to the **full infinitive**, so -er/-ir behave the same: comer → **comería**, vivir → **viviría**.
cards.englishPhrase: I would eat at the restaurant.

cloze.prompt: I would eat (conditional)

cards.english: I would have to work more. (irregular conditional)
cards.grammarNote: Some verbs use an **irregular stem** — the *same* stem as the future — then add **-ía**. tener → **tendría**, hacer → **haría**, poder → **podría**, salir → **saldría**, decir → **diría**.
cards.englishPhrase: I would have to work more.

table.title: Irregular conditional stems (same as future) + -ía
table.note: Learn the stem once; future and conditional share it.

cards.english: I want a coffee vs. I would like a coffee
cards.grammarNote: The **conditional softens** requests to sound polite. Blunt: **quiero** (I want). Polite: **me gustaría** (I would like), **¿podrías...?** (could you...?).
cards.englishPhrase: I want a coffee → I would like a coffee, please.

cards.englishPhrase: I would eat, I would drink, I would live.

cards.english: I will eat vs. I would eat
cards.grammarNote: Future and conditional share the same stem; only the endings differ. Future **-é** = 'will' (comeré). Conditional **-ía** = 'would' (comería).

cards.english: Direct object pronouns — the full set (me / te / lo·la / nos / los·las)
cards.grammarNote:
A **direct object** receives the action of the verb. Replace it with a **direct object pronoun** that matches the person (and gender/number for third person). The pronoun goes **before** the conjugated verb.

**¿El café? Lo quiero.** → *lo* replaces *el café*.

table.title: Direct object pronouns
table.note: lo/la and los/las must match the gender and number of the noun they replace.

cards.english: lo/la replaces a noun to avoid repetition (it — the bread / the salad)
cards.grammarNote:
To avoid repeating a noun, replace it with **lo** (masculine) or **la** (feminine). The pronoun goes **before** the conjugated verb.

*Compro el pan.* → **Lo** compro. | *Compro la ensalada.* → **La** compro.
cards.englishPhrase: I buy the bread. → I buy it.

cloze.prompt: it (the bread — masculine)

cards.english: lo/la/los/las must match the gender AND number of the noun replaced
cards.grammarNote:
**lo** = masc. singular (el pan, el queso…)
**la** = fem. singular (la ensalada, la leche…)
**los** = masc. plural (los huevos, los platos…)
**las** = fem. plural (las galletas, las manzanas…)

Always match the replaced noun, not the English 'it/them'.
cards.englishPhrase: The bread — I want it. The salad — I want it. The cookies — I want them.
cards.phrase: El pan — lo quiero. La ensalada — la quiero. Las galletas — las quiero.

produce.task: Give the correct pronoun for: the bread (masc. sg.), the salad (fem. sg.), the cookies (fem. pl.)
produce.gloss: lo → masc. sg. | la → fem. sg. | las → fem. pl.

cards.english: Pronoun placement: before a conjugated verb OR attached to an infinitive (both correct)
cards.grammarNote:
With **conjugated verb + infinitive**, the direct object pronoun has two equally correct positions:
1. **Before the conjugated verb**: *Lo quiero comprar.*
2. **Attached to the infinitive**: *Quiero comprarlo.*

Both mean the same thing.

contrast.prompt: Both are correct — where does 'lo' go?

cards.english: With estar + gerund, pronoun attaches to the gerund (with accent) OR goes before estar
cards.grammarNote:
With **estar + gerund**, the direct object pronoun has two positions:
1. **Before estar**: *Lo estoy mirando.*
2. **Attached to the gerund** (written accent required): *Estoy **mirándolo**.*

When you attach the pronoun, add an accent to keep the original stress on the gerund.

cloze.prompt: I am watching it — attach the pronoun to the gerund

cards.grammarNote: The **indirect object pronoun** marks the recipient — 'to/for whom'. It goes **before** the conjugated verb. **me** = to me, **te** = to you, **le** = to him/her/usted, **nos** = to us, **les** = to them.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the menu to him (the waiter).
cards.phrase: Le doy el menú al camarero.

table.title: Indirect Object Pronouns
table.note: Pronoun goes before the conjugated verb.

cards.english: le = to him/her with dar and decir
cards.grammarNote: Use **le** when the recipient is 'him', 'her', or 'usted'. It always goes **before** the verb: **le** doy, **le** digo, **le** escribo.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the cake to María.
cards.phrase: Le doy el pastel a María.

cloze.prompt: to her (María) — I give the cake

cards.word: Le doy el café a María.
cards.grammarNote: In Spanish, **le** and **a + person** are used **together**. The pronoun (le/les) is required even when you also name the person with 'a'. This is normal, not redundant.
cards.englishPhrase: I give the coffee to María.
cards.phrase: Le doy el café a María.

produce.task: Say 'I give the coffee to María' — use both le and a María.
produce.answer: Le doy el café a María.
produce.gloss: le + a María together is normal in Spanish — the pronoun is never dropped

cards.english: gustar in reverse: IO pronoun marks who likes it
cards.word: me gusta / te gusta / le gusta
cards.grammarNote: With **gustar**, the thing liked is the **subject** (gusta = singular, gustan = plural). The IO pronoun marks **who** likes it. So: 'I like coffee' = **me gusta** el café (literally: coffee pleases me).
cards.phrase: A ella le gusta el café.

table.title: gustar — reverse verb
table.note: gusta = one thing liked; gustan = multiple things liked.

cards.english: doler (to hurt) follows the same pattern as gustar
cards.grammarNote: **doler** works like gustar — the IO pronoun marks who feels the pain, and the verb agrees with the body part. **me duele** (one part) vs. **me duelen** (plural: los pies, las manos).
cards.phrase: Me duele la cabeza. (Me duelen los pies.)

cloze.prompt: hurts — my head (singular body part)

cards.english: lo (direct) vs. le (indirect): sees him vs. gives to him
cards.word: lo veo / le doy el café
cards.grammarNote: **lo** = direct object — the person/thing directly receiving the action (who/what is seen, bought, etc.). **le** = indirect object — the recipient of something ('to/for whom'). When you give, say, or write *something* **to** someone, that 'someone' gets **le**.
cards.englishPhrase: I see him; I give him the coffee.
cards.phrase: Lo veo; le doy el café.

contrast.prompt: Which pronoun: sees him (direct) or gives to him (indirect)?

b.gloss: I give him the coffee → indirect object / recipient (le)

cards.english: Double object pronouns: indirect always comes first
cards.word: me lo / te la / nos los
cards.grammarNote: When a sentence has TWO object pronouns, the **indirect pronoun comes first**, then the direct: **indirect + direct**.
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee? The waiter gives it to me.
cards.phrase: ¿El café? Me lo da el camarero.

table.title: Two pronouns: indirect + direct
table.note: Order is always: indirect first, then direct.

cards.english: le/les + lo/la → se lo / se la (never le lo)
cards.grammarNote: When **le** or **les** appears before **lo / la / los / las**, the **le/les becomes se**. **Le lo** is never allowed → always **se lo**.
cards.englishPhrase: The menu? I give it to María.
cards.phrase: ¿El menú? Se lo doy a María.

cloze.prompt: to her (María) + it
cloze.text: El menú, a María → ___ lo doy.

cards.word: se lo doy / se lo dice
cards.grammarNote: **le** or **les** + **lo/la** → **se lo / se la**. The indirect object can be clarified with 'a + name': **se lo doy a María**.
cards.englishPhrase: I give it (the coffee) to María. He tells it to her.
cards.phrase: Se lo doy a María. Él se lo dice.

produce.task: Give it (the coffee) to María; tell it to her.
produce.answer: Se lo doy a María. Él se lo dice.
produce.gloss: le + lo is never allowed → se lo; indirect always first

cards.english: Double pronouns: before conjugated verb OR attached to infinitive
cards.word: te lo quiero dar / quiero dártelo
cards.grammarNote: With an infinitive, both pronouns can go **before the conjugated verb** (separate) or **attached together to the infinitive** (add written accent).
cards.englishPhrase: I want to give it to you.
cards.phrase: Te lo quiero dar. / Quiero dártelo.

contrast.prompt: Where do the double pronouns go with an infinitive?

cards.english: Full production: order + se lo rule together
cards.word: te lo compro / se la doy
cards.grammarNote: Combine both rules: **indirect first + direct second**, and **le → se** before lo/la. El pastel (masc.) → **lo**; la cuenta (fem.) → **la**.
cards.englishPhrase: I buy it (the cake) for you. I give it (the bill) to the waiter.
cards.phrase: Te lo compro. Se la doy al camarero.

produce.task: I buy it (the cake) for you; I give it (the bill) to the waiter.
produce.answer: Te lo compro. Se la doy al camarero.
produce.gloss: el pastel → lo (masc.); la cuenta → la (fem.); le + la → se la

cards.grammarNote:
**para** points forward to a **goal, recipient, deadline, or destination** — the finish line ahead.

Wherever PARA appears, something is aimed *at* a target.
cards.englishPhrase: I study in order to learn Spanish.

table.title: Uses of PARA
table.note: All four uses share one idea: PARA aims at a target ahead.

cards.grammarNote:
Use **para + infinitive** to express *purpose* — the goal of an action.

**para** is the one that points to the goal ahead; por is not used for purpose.
cards.englishPhrase: I study in order to learn Spanish.

cloze.prompt: in order to (purpose)

cards.grammarNote:
Use **para + person** to say something is *for* someone — the intended recipient.

The item is aimed at that person.

produce.task: Say: The coffee is for María.
produce.gloss: para + person = the item is intended for that person

cards.grammarNote:
Use **para + time expression** to say something is needed *by* a certain point.

The deadline is the finish line — **para** points straight to it.
cards.englishPhrase: I need the bread by tomorrow.

cloze.prompt: by when (deadline)

cards.grammarNote:
Use **para + place** when you are *heading toward* a destination.

The place is the target you are moving toward — the finish line of your journey.

cloze.prompt: headed toward a destination

cards.grammarNote:
**por** looks back at the **cause or reason**, covers **exchange** and **gratitude**, marks **duration or time of day**, and shows **movement through** a place.

Think: *the motive / the route / the span.*

table.title: Uses of POR
table.note: All four uses share one idea: por points to the motive, the route, or the span — never the goal.

cards.grammarNote:
Use **por** when you name the **cause or reason** behind something — the thing that triggered it.

*Gracias por la comida* → thanks *because of / for* the food.

por looks *back* at the cause; para looks *forward* at a goal.

cloze.prompt: for (cause / reason)

cards.grammarNote:
**por** marks an **exchange** — something given or received *in return for* something else.

Gratitude (*gracias*) is a special case: you give thanks *in return for* what you received.

Pattern: **gracias + por + thing**.

produce.task: Say: Thanks for the bread.

cards.grammarNote:
Use **por** to say *when* or *during what part of the day* something happens.

**por la mañana** = in the morning · **por la noche** = at night.

Think of **por** as covering a **span of time** — not a deadline or destination.

cloze.prompt: during / in the (time of day)

cards.english: POR = movement through / along a place
cards.grammarNote:
Use **por** when you move **through** or **along** a place — the place is the route, not the destination.

*Camino por el parque* → I walk **through** the park.

With *para* it would mean going **to** the park (destination). por = the route; para = the goal.

table.title: POR = through / along (movement)
table.note: The place is the route, not the destination. Switch to para and it becomes the goal.

cards.english: POR — fixed expressions you already know
cards.grammarNote:
Several everyday phrases you already use are built with **por**.

They fit the same pattern: **por** points to a reason, a span, or an exchange — even inside fixed expressions.
cards.englishPhrase: Please, why do you work at night?
cards.phrase: Por favor, ¿por qué trabajas por la noche?

table.title: Fixed POR expressions
table.note: Every phrase uses por because it points to a cause, a span, or an exchange — the same core idea.

cards.english: por vs para — the core mental model
cards.grammarNote:
**PARA** points **forward**: goal, destination, recipient, deadline.

**POR** looks **backward or through**: cause, exchange, duration, route.

Memory hook: PARA = *purpose ahead*; POR = *reason behind / path through*.
cards.englishPhrase: The food is for María. / Thanks for the food.
cards.phrase: La comida es para María. / Gracias por la comida.

contrast.prompt: Which direction does each preposition point?

b.gloss: backward / through — cause / exchange / duration / route

cards.english: trabajar por vs trabajar para — minimal pair
cards.grammarNote:
**Trabajo por María** = I work *because of / on behalf of* María (the motive behind the action).

**Trabajo para María** = I work *for* María (she is my employer / the beneficiary — the goal ahead).

por = the reason; para = the employer / beneficiary.
cards.englishPhrase: I work on behalf of María.

cloze.prompt: I work on behalf of / because of María (motive — not employer)

cards.grammarNote:
When the next word is an **infinitive** and the meaning is *in order to*, use **para**.

**para** + infinitive = goal / purpose ahead. **por** + infinitive would mean *because of doing* — a cause, not a goal.
cards.englishPhrase: I study in order to learn Spanish.

cloze.prompt: I study in order to learn Spanish (purpose)

cards.english: por = route through / para = destination toward
cards.grammarNote:
**por** = movement *through* or *along* a place (you pass through it).

**para** = movement *toward* a destination (that is where you are headed).

Same place, opposite meanings: *por el parque* = through the park; *para el parque* = toward the park.
cards.englishPhrase: I walk through the park. / I leave for the park.
cards.phrase: Camino por el parque. / Salgo para el parque.

contrast.prompt: Same place — passing through it or heading toward it?

b.gloss: destination — the park is where you are headed

cards.grammarNote:
**Gracias por** = thanks *for* something already given → exchange (por looks back).

**Es para** = it is *for* someone → recipient (para points forward).

Two of the most common por/para patterns — learn these as anchors.
cards.englishPhrase: Thanks for the coffee. / The coffee is for María.
cards.phrase: Gracias por el café. / El café es para María.

produce.task: Say: 'Thanks for the coffee' (por — exchange) and 'The coffee is for María' (para — recipient).
produce.answer: Gracias por el café. / El café es para María.

cards.english: Informal commands (tú): use the él/ella form
cards.grammarNote:
For an affirmative **tú** command, just use the **él/ella** present-tense form:
**hablar → habla** (speak!), **comer → come** (eat!), **escribir → escribe** (write!).

table.title: Affirmative tú commands
table.note: Same form as él/ella in the present. Works for regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs.

cards.english: Turn 'to help' into a tú command
cards.grammarNote:
Drop the infinitive ending and use the él/ella form:
**ayudar → ayuda** (help!), **caminar → camina** (walk!), **comprar → compra** (buy!).

produce.concept: Affirmative tú command = él/ella present form
produce.task: Give the tú command for 'estudiar' and 'comprar'

cards.english: Negative tú commands flip the vowel
cards.grammarNote:
For a **negative tú** command, use the subjunctive: take the **yo** form, drop **-o**, and add the *opposite* vowel.
**-ar → -es**: no hables. **-er/-ir → -as**: no comas, no escribas.

table.title: Negative tú commands
table.note: -ar verbs take -es; -er and -ir verbs take -as. The opposite vowel from the affirmative.

cards.grammarNote:
Affirmative and negative **tú** commands use different forms:
affirmative = él/ella form (**come**); negative = subjunctive (**no comas**).

cards.word: di, haz, ve, ven, sal, ten
cards.grammarNote:
Eight common verbs have short irregular **tú** commands. Memorise them:
**decir → di**, **hacer → haz**, **ir → ve**, **venir → ven**, **salir → sal**, **tener → ten**.

table.title: Irregular tú commands
table.note: These irregulars apply only to the affirmative tú command.

cards.grammarNote:
Two easy irregulars to confuse:
**ve** = go! (ir), **ven** = come! (venir). The extra **n** means 'come'.

For a polite **usted** command, use the subjunctive form (yo-stem + opposite vowel):
**hablar → hable**, **comer → coma**, **escribir → escriba**. Same form for affirmative and negative.

table.title: Formal usted commands
table.note: -ar → -e, -er/-ir → -a. For 'don't', just add no: no hable.

cards.english: Speak! — to a friend vs a stranger
cards.grammarNote:
Choose the register:
**habla** (tú) for a friend; **hable** (usted) for a stranger, elder, or in a formal setting.

To say **let's do something**, use the nosotros subjunctive:
**comer → comamos** (let's eat), **hablar → hablemos** (let's talk), **cocinar → cocinemos** (let's cook).

table.title: Nosotros 'let's' commands
table.note: -ar → -emos, -er/-ir → -amos.

cards.grammarNote:
Both mean 'let's eat':
**comamos** (subjunctive) is more formal/written; **vamos a comer** (vamos a + infinitive) is more common in speech.

In **affirmative** commands, object/reflexive pronouns attach to the end of the verb (often adding an accent):
**ayuda + me → ayúdame** (help me), **di + me + lo → dímelo** (tell me it).

table.title: Pronoun attachment (affirmative)
table.note: Pronouns join the end of affirmative commands. An accent keeps the original stress.

cards.english: Where does the pronoun go in a negative command?
cards.grammarNote:
Placement flips with negation:
affirmative → attached (**ayúdame**); negative → **before** the verb (**no me ayudes**).

cloze.prompt: don't help me (pronoun before the verb)

cards.grammarNote:
Reflexive verbs attach the reflexive pronoun in affirmative commands:
**relajarse → relájate** (relax!), **quedarse → quédate** (stay!). Negative: **no te relajes**.

table.title: Reflexive tú commands
table.note: Note: the -te attaches on affirmative commands; negative moves it before the verb (no te quedes).

cards.grammarNote:
The **usted** form is the same for yes and no — just add **no**:
**hable → no hable**, **coma → no coma**, **salga → no salga**.

produce.concept: Negative usted = no + the usted command
produce.task: Make 'coma' and 'trabaje' negative (usted)
produce.gloss: The formal form doesn't change; just add no.

cards.grammarNote: **hacer** has the irregular affirmative command **haz** (not 'hace').

cloze.prompt: do your work! (irregular tú command of hacer)

cards.grammarNote:
The present perfect = **haber** (present) + past participle.
Learn **haber**: he, has, ha, hemos, han. It is only a helper here — 'to have' as in *possession* is **tener**.

table.title: haber — present tense
table.note: haber is the helper for perfect tenses; do not confuse it with tener (to have/own).

cards.grammarNote:
Form the participle from the infinitive:
**-ar → -ado** (hablar → hablado), **-er/-ir → -ido** (comer → comido, vivir → vivido).

table.title: Regular participles
table.note: -ar verbs → -ado; -er and -ir verbs → -ido.

cards.grammarNote:
Put the helper and participle together:
**he + hablado = he hablado** (I have spoken). The participle never changes for gender or number after haber.

produce.task: Say 'we have eaten' and 'she has lived'

cards.grammarNote:
Only **haber** changes with the subject; the participle stays fixed:
**yo he comido**, **ella ha comido**, **ellos han comido**.

cloze.prompt: she has cooked (él/ella form of haber)

cards.word: hecho, dicho, visto, vuelto, escrito, frito
cards.grammarNote:
Some common verbs have irregular participles — memorise them:
**hacer → hecho**, **decir → dicho**, **ver → visto**, **volver → vuelto**, **escribir → escrito**, **freír → frito**.

table.title: Irregular participles
table.note: These don't follow -ado/-ido. Learn them as fixed forms.

cards.english: Pick the correct participle of hacer
cards.grammarNote: **hacer** → **hecho**, never 'hacido'.

cloze.prompt: what have you done? (participle of hacer)

cards.english: Say 'I have seen' and 'I have said'
cards.grammarNote:
Use the irregular participles:
**ver → visto** (he visto), **decir → dicho** (he dicho).
cards.englishPhrase: I have already seen the museum.

produce.task: Say 'she has written' and 'they have returned'

cards.english: The participle never agrees after haber
cards.grammarNote:
After **haber**, the participle always ends in **-o** — it does *not* agree with the subject:
✓ ella ha **comido**, ✗ ella ha ~~comida~~.

The past perfect ('had done') = **haber in the imperfect** + participle:
**había comido** (I had eaten). Forms: había, habías, había, habíamos, habían.

table.title: haber — imperfect (for past perfect)
table.note: Same participles as the present perfect — only the helper changes to the imperfect.

cards.grammarNote:
Choose the helper's tense:
**he comido** = I have eaten (up to now); **había comido** = I had eaten (before another past moment).
cards.englishPhrase: When you arrived, I had already eaten.

b.gloss: had eaten — before another past event

cards.grammarNote:
Past perfect uses the imperfect of haber:
**nosotros habíamos vivido** (we had lived).

cloze.prompt: we had lived (nosotros, past perfect)

cards.grammarNote:
With a reflexive verb, the pronoun goes **before haber**:
**me he relajado** (I have relaxed), **se ha quedado** (he has stayed). Never attach it to the participle.

table.title: Reflexive present perfect (relajarse)
table.note: The reflexive pronoun sits before haber, not attached to the participle.

cards.grammarNote:
The present perfect pairs naturally with time frames that include *now*, like **hoy** (today):
**hoy he trabajado mucho** (today I have worked a lot).
cards.englishPhrase: Today I have worked a lot.

cloze.prompt: today I have worked (yo, present perfect)

cards.english: Recap: build a present perfect sentence
cards.grammarNote:
haber (present) + participle. Remember the irregulars:
**volver → vuelto**, so 'we have returned' = **hemos vuelto**.

produce.concept: Present perfect with an irregular participle
produce.task: Say 'they have returned' and 'I have made dinner'
produce.answer: han vuelto / he hecho la cena

cards.english: How to build the present subjunctive
cards.grammarNote:
Start from the **yo** form, drop the **-o**, and add the *opposite* vowel endings:
**-ar** verbs take **-e** endings; **-er/-ir** verbs take **-a** endings.

table.title: The 'opposite vowel' rule
table.note: -ar → e endings, -er/-ir → a endings. The yo-stem carries any irregularity.

cards.grammarNote:
For **-ar** verbs, the subjunctive endings are **-e / -es / -e / -emos / -en**:
**hable, hables, hable, hablemos, hablen**.

table.title: hablar — present subjunctive
table.note: Same -e endings for all regular -ar verbs: trabajar, cocinar, estudiar, ayudar.

cards.grammarNote:
For **-er/-ir** verbs, the endings are **-a / -as / -a / -amos / -an**:
**comer → coma...**, **vivir → viva...**.
cards.englishPhrase: I want you to eat well.

table.title: comer — present subjunctive
table.note: -er and -ir verbs share these -a endings: comer, vivir, escribir, aprender.

cards.english: Form the subjunctive of a regular verb
cards.grammarNote:
Drop the -o from the yo form and add the opposite vowel:
**trabajar → trabaje**, **vivir → viva**.

produce.task: Give the tú subjunctive of 'estudiar' and 'aprender'

cards.english: Irregular yo-stem carries into the subjunctive
cards.grammarNote:
Verbs with an irregular **yo** form keep that stem in the subjunctive:
**tengo → tenga**, **hago → haga**, **digo → diga**, **salgo → salga**, **conozco → conozca**.

table.title: Yo-stem irregulars
table.note: Take the yo form, drop -o, add -a endings. The whole set follows: tenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengan.

cards.english: Use the yo-stem in the subjunctive
cards.grammarNote: **hacer** → yo **hago** → subjunctive **haga/hagas...** (never 'haces' here).
cards.englishPhrase: I want you to do the exercise.

cloze.prompt: I want you to do it (tú subjunctive of hacer)

cards.grammarNote:
A few verbs are simply irregular — memorise them:
**ser → sea**, **ir → vaya**, **estar → esté**, **dar → dé**, **saber → sepa**, **haber → haya**.

table.title: Irregular subjunctives
table.note: These don't come from the yo-stem. Learn them as fixed forms.

cards.english: Pick the irregular subjunctive of ir
cards.grammarNote: **ir** → subjunctive **vaya** (not 'va').
cards.englishPhrase: I want you to go to the park.

cloze.prompt: I want you to go (tú subjunctive of ir)

cards.word: creo que viene / quiero que venga
cards.grammarNote:
The subjunctive appears after **que** when one subject wants/hopes/needs another to do something:
statement of fact → indicative (**pienso que viene**); wish about someone else → subjunctive (**quiero que venga**).
cards.englishPhrase: I want you to come home.

cards.grammarNote:
Verbs of wishing take the subjunctive when the subject changes:
**quiero que comas** (I want you to eat), **espero que trabajes** (I hope you work).

table.title: Wish triggers + que + subjunctive
table.note: Wanting or hoping that someone else does something forces the subjunctive.

cards.grammarNote:
Wish verb + **que** + subjunctive:
**quiero + que + comas** = I want you to eat.

produce.task: Say 'I hope you speak' and 'I want her to come'
produce.answer: espero que hables / quiero que venga

cards.grammarNote:
No 'que' when the subject doesn't change — use the infinitive:
**quiero comer** (I want to eat, myself) vs **quiero que comas** (I want *you* to eat).

Impersonal phrases of importance/necessity take the subjunctive:
**es importante que...**, **es necesario que...**, **es bueno que...** + subjunctive.

table.title: Impersonal triggers
table.note: These value judgements about someone's action all take the subjunctive.

cards.grammarNote:
**ojalá** means 'hopefully / let's hope' and is always followed by the subjunctive:
**ojalá venga** (I hope he comes), **ojalá vengas** (I hope you come).

cloze.prompt: hopefully she comes (subjunctive of venir)

cards.grammarNote:
When you react emotionally to what *someone else* does, use the subjunctive after **que**:
**me gusta que...**, **es triste que...**, **estoy feliz de que...** + subjunctive.

table.title: Emotion triggers + subjunctive
table.note: Feelings about another person's action take the subjunctive, just like wishes.

cards.grammarNote: **estar** → subjunctive **esté/estés**. After an emotion + que, use it.
cards.englishPhrase: I like that you are happy.

cloze.prompt: I like that you are happy (tú subjunctive of estar)

cards.word: sé que viene / me gusta que venga
cards.grammarNote:
Knowing a fact stays indicative; reacting emotionally turns subjunctive:
**sé que viene** (I know he's coming) vs **me gusta que venga** (I'm glad he's coming).

cards.english: Doubt and denial trigger the subjunctive
cards.grammarNote:
Doubting or denying something takes the subjunctive:
**no pienso que...** (I don't think that...), **tal vez...** (maybe...) + subjunctive.
cards.englishPhrase: I don't think he's coming today.

table.title: Doubt / denial triggers
table.note: Denying or doubting an action pushes the verb into the subjunctive.

cards.english: I think... vs I don't think...
cards.word: pienso que viene / no pienso que venga
cards.grammarNote:
Affirmed belief = indicative; denied belief = subjunctive:
**pienso que viene** (I think he's coming) → **no pienso que venga** (I don't think he's coming).
cards.englishPhrase: I don't think she works today.

cards.grammarNote:
**tal vez** (maybe) expresses doubt, so it usually takes the subjunctive:
**tal vez venga** (maybe he'll come), **tal vez llueva** (maybe it'll rain).

cloze.prompt: maybe she comes (subjunctive of venir)

cards.word: para que, antes de que, sin que
cards.grammarNote:
Some conjunctions are *always* followed by the subjunctive:
**para que** (so that), **antes de que** (before), **sin que** (without).
cards.englishPhrase: I'll help you so that you learn.

table.title: Always-subjunctive conjunctions
table.note: These connectors introduce something not-yet-real, so they always take the subjunctive.

cards.grammarNote: **para que** always triggers the subjunctive: **aprender → aprendas**.
cards.englishPhrase: I explain it so that you understand.

cloze.prompt: so that you understand (tú subjunctive of entender)

cards.english: para + infinitive vs para que + subjunctive
cards.grammarNote:
Same subject → **para** + infinitive; different subject → **para que** + subjunctive:
**trabajo para comer** (I work to eat) vs **trabajo para que comas** (I work so *you* eat).
cards.englishPhrase: I cook so that you eat well.

cards.grammarNote:
After **cuando**, the mood depends on time:
future/not-yet-happened → subjunctive (**cuando llegue**); habitual/routine → indicative (**cuando llego**).
cards.englishPhrase: When I arrive, I'll call you.

table.title: cuando + which mood?
table.note: Not-yet-real future → subjunctive; every-day routine → indicative.

cards.grammarNote:
A future 'when' clause uses the subjunctive:
**cuando vengas** (when you come — hasn't happened yet).

cloze.prompt: when you come (future → subjunctive of venir)

cards.grammarNote:
Routine stays indicative; a one-off future stays subjunctive:
**cuando llego a casa, como** (whenever I get home, I eat) vs **cuando llegue, comeré** (when I get there, I'll eat).
cards.englishPhrase: When I get home, I always eat.
cards.phrase: Cuando llego a casa, siempre como.

cards.grammarNote:
**para que** + subjunctive expresses purpose toward another person:
**te ayudo para que aprendas** (I help you so you learn).
cards.englishPhrase: I teach so that you learn.

produce.task: Say 'I cook so that you eat' and 'I explain so that you understand'
produce.answer: cocino para que comas / explico para que entiendas

cards.grammarNote:
Denying a fact takes the subjunctive: **ser → sea**.
**no pienso que sea bueno** (I don't think it's good).

cloze.prompt: I don't think it is good (subjunctive of ser)

cards.grammarNote:
**más ... que** = more ... than. Put the adjective in the middle:
**más grande que** (bigger than), **más caliente que** (hotter than). **más** already means 'more'.
cards.phrase: El café está más caliente que el té.

cards.grammarNote:
**menos ... que** = less ... than:
**menos grande que** (less big than), **menos caro que** (less expensive than).
cards.englishPhrase: The tea is less hot than the coffee.
cards.phrase: El té está menos caliente que el café.

cards.grammarNote:
For equality with an adjective, use **tan + adjective + como**:
**tan grande como** (as big as), **tan feliz como** (as happy as).
cards.englishPhrase: She is as happy as me.
cards.phrase: Ella está tan feliz como yo.

cards.grammarNote:
For equality with a verb or quantity, use **tanto como** (as much as):
**trabaja tanto como yo** (he works as much as me). With nouns it agrees: **tanta agua**, **tantos libros**.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat as much as you.

cards.grammarNote:
**mejor** = better (the irregular comparative of **bueno**). Don't say 'más bueno'.
**este café es mejor** (this coffee is better).

**peor** = worse (the irregular comparative of **malo**). Don't say 'más malo'.
**la comida está peor hoy** (the food is worse today).

**mayor** = older (for people's age). Use it instead of 'más viejo' for people:
**mi hermano es mayor** (my brother is older).

**menor** = younger (for people's age). Use it instead of 'más joven' for people:
**mi hermana es menor** (my sister is younger).

The superlative = **el/la + más + adjective (+ de)**:
**el más grande** (the biggest), **la más feliz del equipo** (the happiest on the team).
cards.englishPhrase: It's the biggest park in the city.
cards.phrase: Es el parque más grande de la ciudad.

cards.grammarNote:
**el/la mejor** = the best; **el/la peor** = the worst. Add **de** for the group:
**el mejor restaurante de la ciudad** (the best restaurant in the city).
cards.englishPhrase: It's the best coffee in the neighborhood.
cards.phrase: Es el mejor café del barrio.

cards.grammarNote:
Build a comparison as **más/menos + adjective + que**:
**más grande que** (bigger than), **menos frío que** (less cold than).
cards.englishPhrase: The coffee is bigger than the tea.
cards.phrase: El café es más grande que el té.

table.title: Comparison patterns
table.note: más/menos take que; tan/tanto take como.

cards.grammarNote:
Four adjectives have irregular comparatives — don't use más:
**bueno → mejor**, **malo → peor**, **viejo → mayor**, **joven → menor**.
cards.englishPhrase: This coffee is better than that one.
cards.phrase: Este café es mejor que ese.

cards.grammarNote: Equality with an adjective = **tan + adjective + como**. The pair is tan...como, not tan...que.
cards.englishPhrase: I am as tired as you.

cloze.prompt: as tired as you (equality pair)

cards.grammarNote:
For **people's age**, use mayor/menor; for physical **size**, use más grande / más pequeño:
**mi hermano es mayor** (older) vs **esta casa es más grande** (bigger).
cards.englishPhrase: She is older, but I'm bigger.
cards.phrase: Ella es mayor, pero yo soy más grande.

cards.grammarNote:
Superlative = **el/la + más + adjective + de + group**:
**el parque más grande de la ciudad** (the biggest park in the city).
cards.englishPhrase: She's the happiest on the team.
cards.phrase: Ella es la más feliz del equipo.

produce.task: Say 'the biggest park in the city'
produce.answer: el parque más grande de la ciudad

cards.grammarNote:
A reflexive verb turns the action back on the subject ('-self'). Each subject has its pronoun:
**me, te, se, nos, se**. The infinitive ends in **-se** (llamarse, sentirse).

table.title: Reflexive pronouns
table.note: The pronoun matches the subject and normally goes right before the verb.

cards.word: me llamo, te llamas, se llama
cards.grammarNote:
Conjugate the verb normally and add the matching pronoun:
**me llamo, te llamas, se llama, nos llamamos, se llaman** (literally 'I call myself...').

table.title: llamarse (to be called)
table.note: The verb ending changes as usual; the pronoun changes with the subject.

cards.grammarNote:
Match the pronoun to the subject, then conjugate:
**relajarse → me relajo** (I relax), **te relajas** (you relax).

produce.task: Say 'I stay home' (quedarse) and 'she worries' (preocuparse)
produce.answer: me quedo en casa / se preocupa

cards.english: Match the pronoun to the subject
cards.grammarNote:
For **nosotros**, the reflexive pronoun is **nos**:
**nos quedamos** (we stay), **nos relajamos** (we relax).

cloze.prompt: we stay (nosotros reflexive pronoun)

cards.word: lavo el plato / me lavo las manos
cards.grammarNote:
Without the pronoun, the action falls on something else; with it, on yourself:
**lavo el plato** (I wash the plate) vs **me lavo las manos** (I wash my hands).
cards.englishPhrase: I wash my hands before eating.
cards.phrase: Me lavo las manos antes de comer.

cards.grammarNote:
**sentirse** describes how you feel; it's reflexive and stem-changes e→ie:
**me siento, te sientes, se siente, nos sentimos, se sienten**.

table.title: sentirse (to feel)
table.note: Follow with an adjective that agrees: me siento cansada (feminine).

cards.grammarNote:
Some verbs shift meaning with the reflexive:
**me preocupa el trabajo** (work worries me) vs **me preocupo por ti** (I worry about you).

For **él/ella**, the reflexive pronoun is **se**:
**se preocupa** (he/she worries), **se queda** (he/she stays).

cloze.prompt: she worries (él/ella reflexive pronoun)

cards.grammarNote:
With an infinitive, the reflexive pronoun can go two ways:
attached to the infinitive (**quiero relajarme**) or before the first verb (**me quiero relajar**). Both are correct.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to relax at home.

table.title: Two correct placements
table.note: With a conjugated verb + infinitive, either attach to the infinitive or move before the first verb.

cards.english: Move the pronoun before the verb
cards.grammarNote:
The two placements are equivalent:
**quiero quedarme** = **me quiero quedar** (I want to stay).

produce.task: Rewrite 'quiero relajarme' with the pronoun before the verb

cards.english: Body parts take the article, not 'my'
cards.grammarNote:
With reflexive verbs and body parts, Spanish uses the article (the reflexive already shows it's yours):
**me lavo las manos** (I wash my hands), not 'mis manos'.

cloze.prompt: I wash my hands (use the article, not 'mis')

cards.grammarNote:
In the plural, a reflexive can mean **each other**:
**nos reunimos** (we meet up), **se encuentran** (they meet each other).

table.title: Reciprocal (each other)
table.note: Plural reflexives often mean 'each other': nos reunimos, se encuentran.

cards.grammarNote:
The reflexive pronoun attaches to affirmative commands but moves before negative ones:
**relájate** (relax!) vs **no te relajes** (don't relax).

Reflexive pronoun (matching the subject) + conjugated verb:
**él se queda en casa** (he stays home).
cards.phrase: Él se queda en casa hoy.

produce.task: Say 'we relax' and 'they get lost'

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish keeps **no** before the verb and adds a second negative after it:
**no como nada** (I don't eat anything — literally 'I don't eat nothing'). Two negatives are correct here.

table.title: no + verb + negative word
table.note: Unlike English, Spanish requires the double negative when a negative word follows the verb.

cards.grammarNote:
**algo** = something; **nada** = nothing.
**¿quieres algo?** (do you want something?) → **no, no quiero nada** (no, I don't want anything).
Keep **no** before the verb and **nada** after: **no como nada** (I don't eat anything).

cloze.prompt: I don't eat anything (nothing)

cards.grammarNote:
For people: **alguien** = somebody, **nadie** = nobody.
**no veo a nadie** (I don't see anybody) — use the personal **a** before people.
cards.phrase: No hay nadie en la oficina.

table.title: People: positive vs negative
table.note: Both refer to people. Use the personal 'a' when they are the object: no veo a nadie.

cards.grammarNote: **¿hay alguien?** (is anyone there?) → **no, no hay nadie** (no, there's nobody).

Add **no** before the verb and the matching negative word:
**veo a alguien → no veo a nadie** (I see somebody → I don't see anybody).

produce.concept: Turn a positive into a double negative
produce.task: Make 'quiero algo' and 'veo a alguien' negative
produce.answer: no quiero nada / no veo a nadie

cards.grammarNote:
**nunca** can go before the verb alone, or after the verb with **no**:
**nunca como carne** = **no como carne nunca** (I never eat meat). Both are correct.

table.title: Two ways to say 'never'
table.note: If the negative word comes before the verb, you drop 'no'.

cards.grammarNote:
When **nunca** goes before the verb, you don't add **no**:
**nunca bebo café** (I never drink coffee), not 'no nunca bebo'.

cloze.prompt: I never drink wine (nunca before the verb)

cards.grammarNote:
**también** = also (positive); **tampoco** = neither / not either (negative):
**yo también** (me too) → **yo tampoco** (me neither).

contrast.prompt: Agreeing with a positive or a negative?

cards.grammarNote:
**ninguno** = none / not any. Before a masculine noun it shortens to **ningún**:
**ningún problema** (no problem), **ninguna idea** (no idea). Usually singular.

table.title: ninguno agreement
table.note: ninguno → ningún before a masculine noun. It's normally used in the singular.

cards.grammarNote:
**algún** = some/any (positive); **ningún** = no/none (negative):
**¿hay algún problema?** → **no, no hay ningún problema**.
Before a feminine noun, use **ninguna**: **no hay ninguna mesa** (there isn't any table).

cloze.prompt: there isn't any table (feminine noun)

cards.grammarNote:
A negative word can follow the verb (with **no**) or lead the sentence (without **no**):
**no viene nadie** = **nadie viene** (nobody comes).

table.title: Two equivalent orders
table.note: Negative before the verb → drop 'no'. Negative after the verb → keep 'no'.

cards.grammarNote:
Move the negative in front of the verb and drop **no**:
**no viene nadie → nadie viene** (nobody comes).

produce.task: Rewrite 'no viene nadie' and 'no come nada' with the negative first

cards.grammarNote:
**nada** can also intensify a negative to mean 'at all':
**no me gusta** (I don't like it) → **no me gusta nada** (I don't like it at all).
cards.englishPhrase: I don't like it at all.

b.gloss: I don't like it at all

cards.grammarNote:
**gustar** literally means 'to be pleasing'. The thing liked is the subject, and an indirect pronoun says to whom:
**me gusta el café** = 'coffee is pleasing to me'.

table.title: The pronoun says who likes it
table.note: me / te / le / nos / les mark who is pleased. The verb agrees with the thing liked, not the person.

cards.grammarNote:
The verb agrees with the **thing liked**:
singular → **me gusta el café**; plural → **me gustan las galletas**.
Plural thing liked → plural verb: **me gustan las frutas** (I like fruit / fruits).

cloze.prompt: I like vegetables (plural thing → verb agrees)

cards.grammarNote:
Pattern: **pronoun + gusta/gustan + el/la/los/las + thing**:
**me gusta el café** (I like coffee).

produce.concept: gustar pattern with the right pronoun
produce.task: Say 'we like the park' and 'they like the beach'
produce.answer: nos gusta el parque / les gusta la playa

cards.grammarNote:
When you like *doing* something, use **gusta + infinitive** — always singular, even with several actions:
**me gusta leer** (I like reading), **me gusta cocinar y comer**.

table.title: gusta + infinitive
table.note: Always gusta (singular) before an infinitive — never gustan.

cards.english: gusta leer vs gustan las galletas
cards.word: me gusta leer / me gustan las galletas
cards.grammarNote:
Infinitive → singular **gusta**; plural noun → **gustan**:
**me gusta leer** (I like to read) vs **me gustan las galletas** (I like cookies).

**doler** follows the same pattern with body parts:
**me duele la cabeza** (my head hurts), **me duelen los pies** (my feet hurt).

table.title: doler (to hurt)
table.note: Like gustar: the verb agrees with the body part, and the pronoun shows whose it is.

cards.english: doler with a plural body part
cards.grammarNote: Plural body part → **duelen**: **me duelen los pies** (my feet hurt).

cloze.prompt: my feet hurt (plural → verb agrees)

cards.grammarNote:
**encantar** works exactly like gustar but stronger — 'to love / adore':
**me encanta el chocolate** (I love chocolate). No 'muy' needed; encantar is already strong.

table.title: encantar (to love)
table.note: Same mechanics as gustar; singular/plural agreement still applies.

cards.grammarNote:
Strength of feeling:
**me gusta** (I like it) < **me encanta** (I love it). Don't say 'me gusta mucho mucho' — use encantar.

**molestar** (to bother/annoy) uses the gustar pattern:
**me molesta el estrés** (stress bothers me), **me molesta el trabajo** (work bothers me).

table.title: molestar (to bother)
table.note: Careful: molestar means 'to bother', not 'to molest'.

cards.grammarNote: For 'him/her', use **le**: **le molesta el estrés** (stress bothers him/her).

cloze.prompt: it bothers her (him/her pronoun)

cards.grammarNote:
**interesar** (to be interesting to someone) uses the same structure:
**me interesa la música** (I'm interested in music), **me interesan las cosas nuevas**.

table.title: interesar (to interest)
table.note: Related to the known adjective 'interesante'. Same gustar mechanics.

cards.grammarNote:
With any gustar-type verb, a plural subject needs the plural verb:
**me duelen los pies**, **me gustan las galletas**, **me encantan los perros**.

produce.task: Say 'I love cookies' and 'my hands hurt'
produce.answer: me encantan las galletas / me duelen las manos

cards.word: a él le gusta / a mí me gusta
cards.grammarNote:
**le/les** are vague, so add **a + person** to clarify or emphasise:
**a él le gusta** (HE likes it), **a mí me gusta** (as for me, I like it).
cards.englishPhrase: He likes coffee, but I like tea.
cards.phrase: A él le gusta el café, pero a mí me gusta el té.

a.gloss: vague — could be he, she, you
